1.note: This is the beginning of something that Yahweh is saying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quotation of Yahweh. The UST models one way to do that.
See how you translated the term “coastlands” in 40:15. Alternate translation: [all you lands]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and let the peoples become strong again]

The implication is that Yahweh is summoning the nations to a legal trial where their dispute with him will be decided. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [let us draw near together for a legal trial]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **judgment**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [let us draw near together so that we can decide what is right]

2.note: Yahweh is using the question form to assert that he himself is the one who has done this. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I have awakened righteousness from the rising {of the sun}, calling it to my foot.]

Here, **righteousness** represents “a righteous conqueror,” the one whom Yahweh has raised up to act righteously. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [a righteous conqueror]

Yahweh is using **the rising of the sun** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the eastern region]
The pronoun **it** refers to the conqueror whom Yahweh has summoned. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [calling this conqueror to his service]

Yahweh is using **to his foot** as a common expression of the culture to mean summoning someone into his service to follow him. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [calling it to follow him]

The pronoun **He** refers to the Yahweh. The possessive pronoun **his** refers to Cyrus. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh places nations before Cyrus]

Here, **to his face** represents this conqueror being in front of an enemy, that is, attacking that enemy in battle. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he enables him to defeat nations when he fights against them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the conqueror defeating kings as if he physically **tramples** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he defeats kings]

The point of this comparison is that just as **dust** is easily scattered and blown away, so the conqueror easily destroys his enemies with **his sword**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He destroys them with his sword as easily as wind scatters dust]

The point of this comparison is that just as **driven straw** is helplessly scattered by the wind, so the conqueror’s enemies are helplessly scattered before **his bow**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [scattered helplessly before his bow]

Here, **his sword** and **his bow** represent “warfare,” the conqueror’s military power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with his military power … with his military strength]

3.note: The pronoun **He** refers to the conqueror, while the pronoun **them** refers to the nations and kings he defeats. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The conqueror pursues the nations and kings]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he passes through safely]

The implication is that the conqueror advances so swiftly that he seems not even to touch the ground with his feet. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [he advances so swiftly that his feet seem not to touch the ground]

4.q: מִֽי פָעַ֣ל וְ⁠עָשָׂ֔ה קֹרֵ֥א הַ⁠דֹּר֖וֹת מֵ⁠רֹ֑אשׁ
4.note: Yahweh is using the question form to assert that he himself is the one who has done this. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I alone have worked and done this, summoning generations from the beginning!]

SPEAKER is using the singular adjective **first** and the plural adjective **lasts** as nouns to mean certain kinds of things. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [with the first thing and with the last things] or [who was present when the first thing happened and who will be present when the last things happen]

Yahweh is referring to all of human history by naming two major components, **the first** (the first thing that happened) and **the lasts** (the last things that will happen). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who have been present throughout all time]

5.note: Isaiah is using the **coastlands** (the edge of the earth by the sea) and **the ends of the earth** to represent the whole earth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. The UST models one way to show the meaning.

Isaiah is using **the ends of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the most distant places in the world.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the most distant places in the world]

The pronoun **they** refers to the people of the coastlands and the distant lands. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the people of the coastlands and distant lands approach and come]

6.note: Here Isaiah is introducing new participants, beginning with **A man**. Your language may have its own way of introducing new participants that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [There is a man who helps his neighbor]

The implication is that these are idol-makers encouraging one another as they make their idols. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Each idol-maker helps his neighbor]

7.q: וַ⁠יְחַזֵּ֤ק חָרָשׁ֙ אֶת צֹרֵ֔ף מַחֲלִ֥יק פַּטִּ֖ישׁ אֶת ה֣וֹלֶם פָּ֑עַם אֹמֵ֤ר לַ⁠דֶּ֨בֶק֙ ט֣וֹב ה֔וּא וַ⁠יְחַזְּקֵ֥⁠הוּ בְ⁠מַסְמְרִ֖ים לֹ֥א יִמּֽוֹט
7.note: These events happen in sequence, one after another. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [First the craftsman strengthens the metalworker, the one smoothing with a hammer, the one striking the anvil, saying about the soldering, “It is good.” Then they strengthen it with nails, that it may not be moved]
The pronoun **they** refers to the workers who are making the idol. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the workers strengthen it]

The expression **be moved** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that it may not fall over]
Here, the word **that** marks **it may not be moved** as the goal or purpose of fastening the idol with nails. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose.
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

8.note: Yahweh is using the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between other peoples, who are afraid, and the people of **Israel**, who do not need to be afraid. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Unlike them, you, Israel]
This is the beginning of something that Yahweh is saying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as a direct quotation of Yahweh. The UST models one way to do that.

Here and in verses 9 and 10 the word **you** is singular because it refers to the nation of Israel personified as an individual. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

Here Yahweh is speaking of the descendants of Abraham as if they were his **seed**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Abraham]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe Abraham, who is characterized by being **my friend**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Abraham, who was a friend to me]

9.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [and told you that you are my servant,]

The terms **from the ends of the earth** and **from its extremities** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [from the farthest parts of the earth, and I have called you]
The pronoun **you** refers to Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [whom I am seizing you, Israel, from the ends of the earth]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe Israel as **my servant**, the one who belongs to him and serves him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [serve me,’]

10.note: Yahweh is saying what he wants Israel to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that you do not fear, for I am with you. I desire that you do not look around] or [You should not fear, for I am with you. You should not look around]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe his relationship with Israel as **your God**, the one they worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [am the God you worship]

Here, **the right hand** represents “strength” or power. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [with my righteous strength]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [with my righteous right hand]

11.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

The terms **have shame** and **be humiliated** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [they will be completely put to shame]

The expression **be humiliated** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will humiliate them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of those who are angry at Israel as if their anger were a fire that had been **kindled**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones who are angry with you]

The expression **having been kindled** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [all of the ones who burned with anger against you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **nought** is nothing at all, so Israel’s enemies will amount to nothing and perish. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Just as nothing is nothing at all, so they too will be nothing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **contention**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the men who contend with you]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the men** who are characterized by their **contention** with you, that is, those who quarrel with you. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the men who contend with you]

12.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **the men** who are characterized by their **quarrel** with you. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the men who quarrel with you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **quarrel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the men who quarrel with you]

The terms **nought** and **nothing** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [like nothing at all]

13.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe his relationship with Israel as **your God**, the one they worship. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [am the God you worship]

Here, the act of **holding your right hand** represents giving help and support. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [helping and supporting you]

Yahweh is saying what he wants Israel to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [You should not fear]

13.q: הָ⁠אֹמֵ֥ר לְ⁠ךָ֛ אַל תִּירָ֖א אֲנִ֥י עֲזַרְתִּֽי⁠ךָ
13.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [the one telling you not to fear, for I myself will help you]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will help** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is making a commitment to help his people. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I myself will help you]

14.note: The word translated as **May you not fear** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [You do not need to fear]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the people of Jacob as if they were a **worm**, emphasizing how weak and lowly they feel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [weak people of Jacob]

Yahweh is using the possessive form **the declaration of Yahweh** to mean the declaration that Yahweh himself makes. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [declares Yahweh and your Redeemer]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will help** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is making a commitment to Israel. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, will help you]

The word **you** is singular here because Yahweh is addressing the **men of Israel** as if that nation were an individual. So use the singular form in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

The implication is that **your Redeemer** and **the Holy One of Israel** are titles for Yahweh himself. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and he is your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel]

15.note: This is the beginning of another part of what Yahweh is saying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

15.q: שַׂמְתִּ֗י⁠ךְ לְ⁠מוֹרַג֙ חָר֣וּץ חָדָ֔שׁ בַּ֖עַל פִּֽיפִיּ֑וֹת
15.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if he were turning Israel into a **sharp, new sledge**, a tool for threshing grain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am making you powerful, able to crush and destroy your enemies]

Here Yahweh is speaking of Israel defeating their enemies as if they would **thresh** them like grain. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will defeat your enemies and crush them]

Here Yahweh is speaking of powerful enemies as if they were **the mountains** and **the hills**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your powerful enemies and crush them, and you will make your strong enemies]

The point of this comparison is that just as **chaff** is light and worthless and easily blown away, so Israel will reduce their enemies to nothing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and you will make the hills as worthless as chaff]

16.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of Israel destroying their enemies as if they would **winnow** them like grain, so that the wind carries them away. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You will destroy them, and they will be scattered]
The pronoun **them** refers to the enemies of Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [You will winnow your enemies]

Even though Yahweh is the one speaking, he refers to himself in the third person as **Yahweh**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [But you, you will be glad in me]

Yahweh uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the fate of Israel’s enemies and the joy of Israel. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [You, however,]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** along with the verb translated as **you will be glad**, which already includes its meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting the fate of the people of Israel, who will rejoice, with the fate of their enemies, who will be scattered. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But you, for your part, will be glad in Yahweh]

17.note: The terms **poor** and **needy** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [The desperately poor]

Yahweh is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [People who are poor and needy]

Yahweh is using **Their tongue** to represent the whole person, who is suffering from thirst. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [They are parched from thirst]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thirst**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is parched because they have no water to drink]

Even though Yahweh is the one speaking, he refers to himself in the third person as **the God of Israel**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I, Yahweh, I will answer them; I am the God of Israel]

18.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and in the midst of the valleys, I will open fountains]

Here Yahweh is speaking of restoring and blessing his people as if he would turn **the wilderness** into **a pool of waters**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will make the wilderness into a well-watered land]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the dry land, I will make into springs of waters]

19.note: These are all kinds of trees that grow in that region: the **cedar**, the **acacia**, the **myrtle**, and the **tree of oil**. If your readers would not be familiar with these kinds of trees, you could use the names of similar trees that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [trees such as the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive]
The word **Arabah** is the name of a place, a dry desert region.

These are all kinds of trees: the **cypress**, the **plane**, and the **box tree**. If your readers would not be familiar with these kinds of trees, you could use the names of similar trees that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [trees of various other kinds]

20.note: Here, the word **that** marks the clause that follows as the goal or purpose of all that Yahweh does. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [in order that]
The pronoun **they** refers to people in general who will witness what Yahweh does. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [that all people may see and know]

Yahweh is using **set to heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean to think about something carefully. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and take to heart]

Here, **the hand of Yahweh** represents “the power of Yahweh.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the power of Yahweh has done this]

21.note: Yahweh is addressing entities that he knows cannot hear him, the gods of other nations, which he knows do not really exist. He is doing this to communicate strongly to the Israelites that these gods cannot tell what happened in the past or what will happen in the future or do anything at all. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this as if Yahweh were speaking directly to the Israelites about these gods, here and in the next three verses. Alternate translation: [Those false gods cannot bring near any case … They cannot bring forth any arguments]

The word **your** and the implied “you” in the imperatives **Bring near** and **Bring forth** are plural because Yahweh is addressing the gods of the other nations. The words “you” and “your” and the implied “you” in imperatives are plural in verses 22 and 24 for the same reason. So use plural forms in your translation if your language marks that distinction.

22.note: Yahweh is using the adjective **The former** as a noun to mean former things, that is, events that happened in the past. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [Events of the past, what]

22.q: יַגִּ֨ישׁוּ֙ וְ⁠יַגִּ֣ידוּ לָ֔⁠נוּ אֵ֖ת אֲשֶׁ֣ר תִּקְרֶ֑ינָה
22.note: This is part of what Yahweh is saying. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh.

Yahweh is saying what he wants the idol to do. See the discussion in the introduction to this book about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [I desire that they bring forth and declare to us] or [They should bring forth and declare to us]
The pronoun **them** refers to the idols and the false gods. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Let the idols bring forth and declare to us]

Yahweh is using **set to our heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean to think about something carefully. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let us think carefully about them, and let us know]

23.note: Here, the word **and** marks the clause that follows as the goal or purpose of declaring the signs. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [to let us know]

Yahweh is using the possessive form **the signs of the afterward** to mean signs that reveal what will happen in the future. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the signs that show what will happen in the future]

The phrase **let us see** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended, “let us fear.” If that is the correct reading, it suggests that the word translated as **let us look around** has the sense “let us be afraid.” You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and let us be afraid and let us fear]

24.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus the listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Look]

Yahweh says **less than nought** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [you {are} utterly worthless]

The implication is that anyone who chooses to worship these idols does something that Yahweh finds detestable. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [He who chooses to worship you does what Yahweh finds detestable]

Here Yahweh is using the pronoun **He** in a general sense, to refer to anyone who chooses to worship the idols, not to a specific person. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone who chooses you is an abomination]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **abomination**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [He who chooses you is someone I hate]

25.note: Here Yahweh refers to a certain person, the conqueror he has summoned, without naming him. Your language may use this construction in the same way. If not, you can translate it with an equivalent phrase that names the person. Alternate translation: [I have awakened a conqueror from the north]

The pronoun **he** refers to the conqueror whom Yahweh has summoned from the north. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [a conqueror from the north, and he comes]

Yahweh is using **From the rising of the sun** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from the east.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [one from the north, and he comes. From the east]

The point of this comparison is that just as a person tramples **mud** underfoot without effort, so the conqueror will easily defeat the **rulers**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he will easily trample rulers as person would trample mud]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a potter treads clay** to shape it however he wishes, so the conqueror will completely subdue the rulers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and as a potter completely subdues clay to shape it however he wishes]
The pronoun **he** refers to the conqueror, while the word **my** refers to Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Cyrus calls upon the name of Yahweh]

Yahweh is using **calls upon my name** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the conqueror acknowledges and honors him. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he honors me]

27.note: Here Yahweh is describing events in the order they happened. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [First I said to Zion, ‘Behold, behold them!’ and then I sent a herald to Jerusalem]

Here Yahweh is speaking of the idols as if they were nothing but **wind and emptiness** to show that they are worthless and powerless.
